headline: Fall River tax board backs agreements tied to 280 proposed housing units
dek: The Oct. 6 votes support redevelopment at a former school, a historic mill and another former school, but the projects still face financing and construction steps.
body: Fall River’s Tax Increment Financing Board unanimously approved tax-increment exemption agreements for three residential redevelopment projects that together describe 280 proposed market-rate homes. The Oct. 6 votes cover a new apartment building at the former Silvia School site, the conversion of the vacant Charlton Mill and a studio project at the former Connell School. The [Fall River Reporter’s account](https://fallriverreporter.com/fall-river-tif-board-approves-tax-agreements-for-three-housing-projects-that-will-bring-over-200-new-units/) said the developers are seeking Massachusetts Housing Development Incentive Program benefits and historic tax credits.

The largest proposal is Charlton Mill Lofts at 109 Howe Street beside Cook Pond. The project calls for a $65 million rehabilitation of the vacant historic mill into 147 rental units, followed by construction of another building with 68 units. The reported unit mix in the mill is 55 studios, 74 one-bedroom apartments and 18 two-bedroom apartments. The new building is described as having 52 one-bedroom, eight two-bedroom and eight three-bedroom units. Together, that project accounts for 215 of the 280 proposed units.

The mill proposal would reuse a building with a documented place in Fall River’s industrial landscape. The Fall River Reporter identified the structure as having been built in 1911 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and the [city’s historic-register materials](https://cms2.revize.com/revize/fallriver/Document%20Center/Goverment/Boards%20%26%20Commissions/Historical%20Commission/Register%20of%20Significant%20Structures-%206.2024.pdf) also identify Charlton Mill at 109 Howe Street. Reusing the site could add housing without putting all of the project’s residential footprint on undeveloped land, but the reporting does not establish when rehabilitation will begin or whether every proposed unit will ultimately be financed and built.

At 138 Hartwell Street, Downtown Lofts, a division of Cordeiro Properties, proposes a new $21 million building called Jenna’s Corner Lofts on the former Frank Silvia School site. The plan includes 49 market-rate rental apartments: 29 one-bedroom units and 20 two-bedroom units. The site was condemned after a March 2025 fire, according to the Fall River Reporter, and the city’s Zoning Board of Appeals granted a special permit in March. The proposal includes 49 on-site parking spaces plus additional spaces at 60 Hartwell Street.

The third agreement covers Cornell Lofts LLC’s proposed $4 million conversion of the former Connell School at 650 Plymouth Avenue into 16 market-rate studio apartments. The three developments therefore represent different kinds of housing redevelopment: new construction on a damaged former school parcel, adaptive reuse of a historic mill and a smaller school conversion. That mix is relevant in a former mill city where vacant or underused buildings can be candidates for housing, but it also means the projects will have different design, preservation and construction risks.

The vote is a tax-incentive step, not an announcement that 280 apartments are ready for occupancy. [Fall River Now’s meeting recording and summary](https://fallrivernow.transistor.fm/episodes/10-6-2026-tax-increment-financing-board) say the board approved 10-year agreements using an 80% exemption for the first five years and 20% for the next five. Under the state’s [Housing Development Incentive Program guidance](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/housing-development-incentive-program-hdip), a Gateway City can use a local-option exemption on all or part of the increased property value created by a qualifying market-rate housing project, alongside a state tax-credit process. The agreements can improve a project’s financing picture, but they do not by themselves settle construction timing, final design or tenant move-in dates.

Massachusetts describes HDIP as a tool for Gateway Cities to increase residential growth, diversify the housing supply, support economic development and stabilize neighborhoods. The state program is aimed at new construction or substantial rehabilitation of multi-unit market-rate housing, and the state says projects generally must contain at least 80% market-rate units. The Fall River agreements were reported as market-rate proposals; the sources reviewed for this article did not identify income-restricted apartments in these three plans or say that affordable units will be added later.

The immediate next questions are practical. The developers must complete the state and local credit processes, secure financing, finalize plans and move through construction before the proposed units can affect Fall River’s housing supply. The public reporting confirms the board’s votes and the projects’ stated scopes, but it does not provide a construction schedule, final rents, a completion date or a tenant-application process. For residents watching the city’s housing pipeline, those milestones will show whether the tax agreements translate into apartments rather than remaining preliminary redevelopment proposals.
author: NorthEast News Desk
